0.0.n: This holiday name is written in katakana, a script often used for borrowed words.

0.1.n: Marks Christmas as the time when people eat chicken.

0.2.n: Highlights Christmas as the topic, following the time particle に.

0.4.n: This borrowed food word refers to chicken meat here.

0.5.n: Marks チキン as what people eat.

0.6.n: The plain form of 食べる directly describes 人: people who eat chicken.

0.7.n: Japanese nouns do not require plural endings; the context makes 人 plural here.

0.8.n: Marks the people who eat chicken as the group described by 多い.

0.9.n: Describes the number of people, rather than going before 人 like English many.

0.10.n: Marks the preceding statement as the content of the speaker's thought.

0.11.n: The polite form of 思う softens the statement by presenting it as the speaker's view.

1.0.n: Sets an earlier period as the background for the speaker's habit.

1.1.n: Makes the past the topic, suggesting a contrast with now.

1.3.n: The speaker explicitly refers to themself here.

1.4.n: Adds the speaker to others who prepared chicken.

1.5.n: Emphasizes that the chicken was not cut into pieces.

1.6.n: Connects 丸ごと to チキン so that it describes the chicken.

1.7.n: Here it refers to a whole bird prepared for eating.

1.8.n: Marks the whole chicken as what the speaker roasted.

1.9.n: 焼い is the changed verb base of 焼く used before たり.

1.10.n: Presents roasting as an example of what the speaker used to do.

1.11.n: The polite past form of している completes たりする and expresses a past habit here.

2.0.n: Introduces another point, rather than referring to a later time.

2.2.n: This is the restaurant chain's name, referring here to its food.

2.3.n: Marks Kentucky Fried Chicken as what people eat.

2.4.n: The plain form directly describes 人, forming people who eat Kentucky Fried Chicken.

2.5.n: The preceding words specify which people the speaker means.

2.6.n: Adds this group as another group that is numerous.

2.7.n: 多い describes a large number, and です makes the statement polite.

3.0.n: Refers to December 24 in this Christmas context; the month is left unstated.

3.1.n: Marks the date when someone passes the restaurant.

3.2.n: This is a common shortened Japanese name for Kentucky Fried Chicken.

3.3.n: Links the restaurant to 前, identifying the space in front of it.

3.4.n: Names the area in front of the restaurant.

3.5.n: Marks the area someone passes through, not an object being acted on.

3.6.n: The plain form combines with と to describe what happens when someone passes.

3.7.n: Connects passing the restaurant with the predictable sight that follows.

3.9.n: Informally emphasizes the impressive size of the queue.

3.10.n: Refers to people lined up waiting, not a drawn line.

3.11.n: Marks the queue as what has formed.

3.12.n: できる plus ています describes the resulting state: the queue has formed and is still there.

0.lit: At Christmas, people who eat chicken are numerous, I think.
0.tip: 食べる人 means people who eat; Japanese puts the description directly before the noun.

1.lit: In the past, I too used to do things like roasting whole chicken.
1.tip: たりしていました presents roasting as an example of a past habit.

2.lit: Also, people who eat Kentucky Fried Chicken are numerous too.
2.tip: 人も多い says there are also many people in this group.

3.lit: On the 24th, when you pass in front of KFC, a huge queue has formed.
3.tip: できています describes an existing queue resulting from people lining up, not an ability to do something.
